title: What is a pointer? A variable that holds an address

visuals.title: Two pointers and two variables (made-up addresses)

steps.note: a and b are ordinary boxes holding numbers.
p is a pointer. It stores the ADDRESS of a (0x1000), shown here as an arrow.
q copies the address inside p. Both arrows point to a.
*q means the box q points to, which is a. a becomes 15.
p now stores the address of b. Its arrow moves. q is not affected.
*p is b, so b becomes 40.
Prints 15 40 40 15.

pairs.meaning: Declaration: p is a pointer to an int

goal: After this you can declare a pointer, make it point to a variable with &, read and change that variable through the pointer with *, and avoid uninitialized and null pointer mistakes.
warmup: In your phone, a contact does not contain the person. It contains a phone number. When you tap it, you reach the person. A pointer is the same idea: the pointer does not contain the data, it contains the address where the data lives. Following the address to reach the data is called dereferencing. Think of a friend who gives you a slip of paper with his house number. The slip is the pointer, the house is the variable.
definition: A pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable. You declare it with a * and the type of thing it points to: int *p; means p can hold the address of an int. p = &x; stores the address of x in p, so p points to x. In an expression, *p means the value stored at the address inside p (dereferencing). You can read through it (cout << *p) and write through it (*p = 75;). Writing through the pointer changes the original variable.
howItWorks: Follow the arrows in the memory picture. First the ordinary variables get values. Then a pointer is created and given an address with &. An arrow shows what it points to. Be careful with the star because it has TWO meanings. In a declaration, int *p; the * only says that p is a pointer. In an expression, *p means go to that address and use what is there. Every pointer has a type: int * points to an int, double * to a double, char * to a char, and the type must match the variable. An uninitialized pointer contains a random address, so using it can crash the program. So start a pointer with an address or with nullptr (this means no address). Before dereferencing a pointer that might be null, check it: if (p != nullptr). Also remember that int *a, b; makes only a a pointer. Write int *a, *b; for two pointers. Finally, a pointer is itself a variable with its own address, and you can point it somewhere else later: p = &b; moves the arrow but changes no variable.

sample.title: Declare a pointer, point it, read and write through it
sample.expectedOutput:
num  = 50
*ptr = 50
ptr holds the address of num? 1
num after *ptr = 75: 75

explanation.text: The * in a declaration means: ptr is a pointer to an int. It will hold an address.
Store the address of num in ptr. Now ptr points to num.
In an expression, *ptr means the value at the address in ptr (dereference). Here it reads 50.
Comparing two addresses. The answer 1 means true.
Writing through the pointer changes num itself.

steps.note: num is an ordinary int box holding 50.
ptr is a pointer to int. Right now it holds no meaningful address, so we must not use it yet.
&num is the address of num. Now ptr holds that address, so we say ptr points to num.
Prints the value in num.
*ptr means: go to the address stored in ptr and read the value there. That is num's value, 50.
ptr contains exactly the address of num, so the comparison is true. true prints as 1.
steps.out: ptr holds the address of num? 1

steps.note: *ptr on the left side means: store 75 in the box ptr points to. That box is num, so num becomes 75.
num was changed through the pointer.

steps.note: Two ordinary boxes: a = 10 and b = 20.
p points to a.
q receives a COPY of the address stored in p. Now both p and q point to a.
*q is a. a was 10, so a becomes 15. p also sees this because it points to the same box.

variations.when: You need a pointer to an int. The * can touch the type or the name: int* p and int *p are the same.
You already know what it points to. The best habit.
You do not know the target yet. Check p != nullptr before use.
You want the value that p points to.
You want to change the original variable.
The pointer type must match the variable type.
Make q point to the same variable as p.

mistakes.error: error: cannot convert 'double*' to 'int*' in initialization

mistakes.wrong:
int *p;
*p = 5;   // p holds a random address
mistakes.error: The compiler may only give a warning (or nothing). At run time the program can crash because p points to a random place. The fix is to point p at a real variable first.
It compiles, but crashes when it runs. Never dereference a null pointer: test it first.

examTips: Definition to write: a pointer is a variable that stores the address of another variable. Add a tiny example: int *p = &x;
Know the two meanings of *: in a declaration it means pointer type; in an expression it means the value at the address (dereference). & means address-of.
When tracing, keep a table of variables. For each pointer write which variable it points to, like p -> a. A change through *p changes the variable it points to.
Remember: p = &b moves the pointer, *p = 5 changes the value. They are different things.
Always initialize pointers (with an address or nullptr) and check for nullptr before dereferencing. Examiners like this sentence.
romanSummary: Pointer aisa variable hai jo kisi doosre variable ka address store karta hai, jaise phone mein contact number store hota hai, banda nahi.
int *p = &x; likhne se p, x ko point karta hai. &x address deta hai.
*p (dereference) se us address par pari value milti hai aur *p = 75 likhne se original variable badal jata hai.
* ke do matlab hain: declaration mein pointer ki alamat, aur expression mein address par pari value.
Pointer ko hamesha initialize karo, ya nullptr do, aur use karne se pehle check karo ke woh nullptr to nahi.

practice.hint: A contact stores a number, not the person.
practice.explanation: A pointer holds an address, and following it (with *) reaches the variable.

practice.explanation: p points to x, so *p = 9 changes x to 9.

practice.hint: Both pointers point to the same variable a.
practice.explanation: a starts at 4. Through p it becomes 5. Through q it becomes 5 x 2 = 10.

practice.prompt: In int *a, b; which names are pointers?

practice.explanation: Only a is a pointer. b is a plain int. Write int *a, *b; for two pointers.

practice.hint: p needs an address, not a value.
practice.explanation: n is an int value; a pointer needs the address of n, written &n.

practice.prompt: Write a program with int score = 40 and a pointer ptr to it. Add 10 to score only through ptr, then print score.

practice.explanation: After the swap of pointers p points to b (8) and q points to a (3). a and b are unchanged: 3 and 8.

quiz.prompt: Which line makes ptr point to num?
quiz.explanation: &num is the address of num, so ptr = &num makes ptr point to it.

quiz.prompt: If ptr points to num, what is *ptr?
quiz.explanation: *ptr is the value stored at the address inside ptr, which is num.

quiz.prompt: What is the safe way to create a pointer that points to nothing yet?
quiz.hint: Choose a value that means no address.
quiz.explanation: nullptr clearly means points to nothing and can be tested.

quiz.prompt: int x = 5; int *p = &x; *p = 8; What is x?
quiz.hint: Writing through the pointer changes x.
quiz.explanation: *p is x itself, so x becomes 8.

quiz.prompt: Why can using an uninitialized pointer crash the program?
options: It holds a random address that may not belong to the program
It holds 0 which is a valid address
quiz.answer: It holds a random address that may not belong to the program
quiz.explanation: An uninitialized pointer contains garbage. Dereferencing it touches memory the program may not own.
